newsitem.title: GERMANY: German firms seek EU injunction against D.Telekom.
newsitem.headline: German firms seek EU injunction against D.Telekom.

text.p: Deutsche Telekom's main German rivals have filed a complaint in Brussels, urging the European Commission to repeal an earlier ruling that allows Telekom to give big discounts to companies, industry sources said on Thursday.
The complaint threatens to spark a new row over a set of controversial tariffs that Telekom's rivals say represent a massive abuse of the company's dominant market position.

The dispute raises new uncertainties about the regulatory environment in Germany just weeks before Deutsche Telekom's international share listing. It could also cast doubt on final approval for Global One, the company's international venture with France Telecom and Sprint Corp.
The tariffs, set to take effect on November 1, offer Telekom's corporate customers discounts for telecommunications services of up to 49 percent based on the call volume.

But the six main companies competing against Telekom in the area of corporate networks now say that the strict conditions set by the European Commission when it approved the rates in June have not been met and should be reviewed.
"We are seeking an injunction in Brussels that will stop the new tariffs from taking effect on November 1," an industry source involved in the matter told Reuters.
"Why should these rates be allowed now if the conditions set by Brussels have not been fulfilled?" he asked.

The complaint was filed by Communications Network International, the Mannesmann unit, Thyssen subsidiary Plus Net, Veba's Meganet, RWE Telliance AG, WorldCom Inc and Viag Interkom, the joint venture of Viag AG and British Telecom.
The companies will outline their complaint at a news conference on Friday in Duesseldorf.

Brussels approved the discounts in June after a lengthy dispute with German Post and Telecommunications Minister Wolfgang Boetsch and only after winning assurance from Bonn that strict conditions would be met.

The German government had to agree that "at least two licences for the construction or ownership and control of alternative infrastructure" offering telecoms services would have come into force by November.

The six companies complain that while Telekom will grant big discounts to its customers, it is charging its competitors inflated prices for leased lines, preventing them from being able to offer competitive services.

If Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert sides with the companies that filed the complaint, it could spark a new row between Bonn and Brussels over just how fast Germany is moving to open its telecommunications sector to competition.
This in turn, said industry sources, could cause the Commission to reassess its approval of Global One.
"These steps could very well have an impact on Global One because the German government is not behaving in a neutral manner that promotes competition," said one source.
When it approved Global One in July, the Commission stated that it could not begin offering services until France and Germany had issued two licenses to alternative networks.
Industry sources said this could mean that the Commission could again exert pressure on Germany and France to take new steps to open markets by threatening to withhold final approval for Global One.
